result: GREM1 expression is upregulated in fibrotic MASH liver tissue in both humans and rats. In human MASH liver, GREM1 was undetectable in healthy liver but increased in fibrotic MASH liver, localizing to fibrotic septa (C1-C3). RTqPCR showed 4.8- to 9.8-fold increases in GREM1 mRNA in various F4 liver diseases compared to donor livers (C4). In the rat CDAA-HFD model, Grem1 ISH staining was consistently increased and localized to periportal and fibrotic areas (C13-C14), with weak protein signal by IHC (C15-C16).
evaluation: All reviewers accepted these findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 noted 'the impressive volume of high-level, well-controlled data' and Reviewer 2 stated 'the authors used RNAscope in situ hybridization to establish the correlation between Gremlin-1 expression and NMSH livers.' The editor described the conclusions as 'supported by a convincing, well-controlled set of experiments.'

result: GREM1 expression does not correlate with histological stage of fibrosis in MASLD patients, based on analysis of publicly available bulk RNA-sequencing data from 352 patients capturing the whole spectrum of MASLD and MASH.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question this finding. The analysis of large public datasets (352 patients across three studies) showing no correlation with fibrosis stage was accepted as part of the overall characterization of GREM1 expression patterns.

result: GREM1 is expressed in myofibroblasts in fibrotic liver tissue, but only in a small, variable subpopulation. GREM1 mRNA-positive cells co-stained with myofibroblast markers THY1 and COL3A1 (C6-C7), with highest expression in primary HHSC and myofibroblasts compared to other hepatic cell types (C8). However, only a small proportion of THY1/COL3A1+ cells expressed GREM1 with high variability (C9-C10). Single-cell RNA-seq analysis confirmed very low overall expression with slightly higher levels in myofibroblast populations (C11-C12).
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as part of the comprehensive characterization. Reviewer 2 specifically noted 'the authors used RNAscope in situ hybridization to establish the correlation between Gremlin-1 expression and NMSH livers or cell lines.' The heterogeneous and restricted expression pattern was not challenged.

result: Gremlin-1 is not detectable in circulation and binds to heparin with high affinity, preventing systemic circulation. The authors could not detect circulating Gremlin-1 in plasma or serum from healthy subjects and MASLD patients (C19) or by LC-MS (C20). Size exclusion chromatography showed Gremlin-1 forms complexes with heparin (C21), suggesting retention on cell surfaces and ECM (C22). Binding affinity to heparin was in the low nanomolar range (13 nM) (C23, C32), suggesting strong ECM localization (C24) and preventing systemic circulation and organ crosstalk (C81-C82).
evaluation: This finding was explicitly praised by all reviewers as a major contribution. The editor stated it 'challenges existing data on the detection of GREM1 by ELISA in serum or plasma by demonstrating that high-affinity binding of GREM1 to heparin would lead to localisation of GREM1 in the ECM or at the plasma membrane.' Reviewer 1 noted 'this paper will challenge many existing papers in the field around our ability to detect GREM1 in circulation.' Reviewer 2 stated 'they found that Gremlin-1 binds to heparin very efficiently, preventing Gremlin-1 from entering circulation.'

result: The generated anti-Gremlin-1 antibodies effectively block Gremlin-1 from binding BMP4 and restoring BMP signaling in vitro. Antibodies showed high efficacy in ELISA (IC50=2.7-3.1×10⁻⁹ M) (C25) and BMP reporter assays (EC50=1.27-1.36×10⁻⁸ M) (C26). They restored SMAD1 phosphorylation blocked by Gremlin-1 (C27-C29). The antibodies differed in binding stoichiometry (C30-C31) and heparin-displacing properties: 0030:HD reduced heparin binding affinity 10-fold (C33-C34) and prevented Gremlin-1 cell surface binding (C35-C36), while 0032:ND did not affect heparin binding (C33, C37). The antibodies formed distinct complexes with Gremlin-1 and heparin (C38-C39).
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the antibody characterization data without challenge. Reviewer 1 described the study as having 'impressive volume of high-level, well-controlled data using an impressive range of in vitro biochemical techniques.' One reviewer raised a concern about 'in-house reagents and assays' lacking 'external validation,' but this was a minor methodological comment rather than a challenge to the antibody efficacy claims.

result: Anti-Gremlin-1 blockade and GREM1 overexpression do not significantly affect fibrotic marker expression in hepatic stellate cells. Anti-Gremlin-1 antibodies did not change COL1A1, ACTA2, or TIMP1 expression in primary HHSC or myofibroblasts (C40). Lentiviral overexpression achieved 177-fold increase in LX-2 and 6.3-fold in HHSC (C41-C42) but did not affect fibrotic markers (C43). GREM1 overexpression modestly increased LOX in vehicle-treated LX-2 only (C44) but not CCL2 or LOXL1 (C45), and affected BMP-related gene expression including reduced BMP4, SMAD6, SMAD7 (C46), reduced INHBB (C47), and increased BMP7 and SMAD1 (C48).
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these negative findings as part of the comprehensive evidence that Gremlin-1 targeting is ineffective. Reviewer 2 stated 'the experimental design and results support the conclusion that the anti-gremlin-1 antibody had no therapeutic effect on treating liver fibrosis.' The changes in BMP-related genes without effects on fibrotic markers were not challenged.

result: Anti-Gremlin-1 antibody treatment does not reduce MASH phenotype in the rat CDAA-HFD model. The CDAA-HFD diet induced expected MASH phenotype with reduced body weight and increased ALT, AST, liver weight, steatosis, fibrosis, and immune infiltrates (C49-C50). Heparin-displacing antibody treatment increased circulating Gremlin-1 (C51), suggesting removal from ECM (C52), but neither heparin-displacing nor non-displacing antibodies changed any MASH phenotype parameters (C53).
evaluation: All reviewers accepted this key negative finding. The editor stated the paper 'shows that the anti-gremlin-1 (GREM1) antibody is not effective at treating liver inflammation or fibrosis.' Reviewer 1 noted the study presents 'data suggesting that the targeting of GREM1 has little impact on a mouse model of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis.' Reviewer 2 stated 'they demonstrated that neutralization of Gremlin-1 activity with monoclonal therapeutic antibodies does not reduce liver inflammation or liver fibrosis.'

result: Anti-Gremlin-1 antibody treatment does not reduce fibrotic markers in human precision-cut liver slices (PCLS). The compounds showed no toxicity (C54). TGFβ1 increased and ALK5 inhibition decreased fibrotic markers as expected (C55-C56), but anti-Gremlin-1 antibody did not reduce COL1A1, ACTA2, or TIMP1 expression (C57) or Pro-collagen 1A1 protein levels (C58). Gremlin-1 protein was not detectable in supernatants (C59), but antibody showed adequate tissue penetration by microscopy (C60). 3'-mRNA-sequencing showed no considerable gene expression changes with anti-Gremlin-1 treatment (C61).
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as strong evidence against therapeutic efficacy. Reviewer 2 specifically mentioned 'they also used human cirrhotic precision-cut liver slices to test their hypotheses' and concluded the antibody 'had no therapeutic effect.' The use of human ex vivo tissue was viewed as a strength of the study.

result: Overall conclusion that Gremlin-1 has a redundant role in liver fibrosis pathogenesis and is unamenable to therapeutic targeting. The authors conclude that neutralization of Gremlin-1 activity does not reduce liver inflammation or fibrosis in multiple model systems (C76). While Gremlin-1 was upregulated in MASH fibrosis (C77), expression was restricted to a small myofibroblast subpopulation (C78). Overexpression led to BMP-related gene changes without increased fibrogenesis (C79-C80). The findings suggest a redundant role (C83) that is unamenable to therapeutic targeting (C84).
evaluation: All reviewers accepted this overall conclusion. The editor called it an 'important paper' with 'convincing, well-controlled' experiments. Reviewer 1 described it as an 'impressive tour-de-force study' and noted 'well-controlled, detailed studies like this are critically important in order to challenge less vigorous studies in the literature.' Reviewer 2 stated 'this manuscript provides useful information that gremlin-1 has a limited role in liver fibrosis pathogenesis and treatment.'
